reasoning: Failure edits were kept in full and take priority. Four anchors were targeted by both groups, so each pair was merged into one insertion to avoid ordering ambiguity. (1) 'do not append that role word': the failure delete-clue-words test and the success head-noun exception are combined, with a clarification that the test strips specific words the clue states ('funeral', 'Poker Flat'), while generic type nouns like 'empire' or 'bomb' follow the head-noun exception. A bare 'one of these' still gets the plain common noun. (2) 'The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.': the failure edits (character-name lists, letter counts, double-meaning clues) and the success edits (date+place fragments, jokes and local-word glosses) are combined. (3) 'asks for the title or category noun itself': the failure 'Modifier type of this' rule and the success set-completion rule are combined. The remaining success edits (epithet clues, forum-thread archive hits, pun-as-confirmation replacement, full standard names for works and kings, series granularity) cover patterns the failure edits do not address and do not conflict with them, so they are kept as separate edits. No edit touches the protected section.

edits.target: asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content:
- 'The <Modifier> type / style / version / kind / variety of this' ('the Denver type of this', 'the Boston version of this', 'the Manhattan kind of this') names a standard compound whose head noun is the answer. Search the passages for '<Modifier> <noun>' (e.g. 'Egg White Denver Omelet', 'Denver omelet') and answer with the bare generic noun ('Omelet'), not the modifier and not a branded or themed product from the passages. A candidate must contain or fit the clue's distinctive modifier. A brand item such as 'Egg White Delight McMuffin' that matches only the side theme (cholesterol, egg whites) is wrong. Other clue details (diet, ingredient, cooking method) are just conditions on the generic dish.
- 'X needs A & one of these' / 'A, B and one of these': the clue already gives some members of a set. Find the passage listing the full set ('a subject and a predicate') and answer with the missing member ('subject'), never one already named in the clue.

edits.target: do not append that role word to the answer.
edits.content:
- DELETE-CLUE-WORDS TEST: before answering, strike from your candidate every specific word or phrase the clue already states, and keep only the remaining head. 'Bret Harte wrote about these exiles "of Poker Flat"' -> 'The Outcasts' (not 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'). 'Robert La Follette called it the Progressive party, but it was nicknamed this' -> 'Bull Moose' (not 'Bull Moose Party'). 'This funeral structure' -> 'Pyre' (not 'funeral pyre', and not 'funeral boat', which echoes the clue's 'funeral' and ignores that the passages say 'funeral pyre').
- When the clue says only 'one of these' / 'this <generic noun>' and the answer is a common noun, give the plain common noun with no added modifiers: 'a back shaped like one of these' -> 'Balloon' (not 'hot air balloon'). Modifiers copied from passages (hot air, synthetic, funeral, speech) are usually wrong unless part of the standard proper name.
- Exception (head noun is part of the standard name): when the clue itself gives a generic type noun ('this empire', 'this gland', 'these bombs') and the bare modifier alone would not name the entity, keep the head noun in the form the passages use. 'this empire' -> 'Roman Empire' (not 'Roman'); 'this gland' -> 'pituitary gland'; 'one of these bombs' -> 'hydrogen bomb'; 'term for a leg cramp' -> 'Charley horse'. The same holds for named events, deals, treaties, wars and laws when the clue gives only a generic descriptor with the head word ('1853 purchase that brought the U.S. to its present area' -> 'Gadsden Purchase', not 'Gadsden'). Test: would a trivia answer key accept the bare word alone? If yes ('Sirius', 'Roanoke', 'Amazon', 'Yalta'), drop the type word. If not, keep the head noun. Pure category labels ('play', 'king', 'spacecraft', 'novel') are still dropped: 'this play' -> 'Henry V'. The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Name form: for a plain biographical clue ('She was convicted in 1976 ...'), use the formal full name that the passages give, not a nickname or diminutive: 'Patricia Hearst', not 'Patty Hearst'. Use the nickname form only when the clue itself uses it. For foreign landmarks, palaces, museums and places, use the standard English name that the clue's wording implies ('Pitti Palace', not 'Palazzo Pitti'; 'Florence', not 'Firenze'), unless a verbatim archive hit shows another form.

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content:
- A clue that is only a list of fictional character names, roles or catchphrases ('Inspector Luger, Wojo, Fish') asks for the WORK they all belong to (the TV series, film, book or play: 'Barney Miller'). Do not answer with one actor, one character, or the list items. Pick the title that every passage pairs with all the names. If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
- A trailing number in parentheses, e.g. 'Flirtatious floozy Flanders (4)', is a crossword-style LETTER COUNT for the answer. The answer MUST have exactly that many letters (ignoring spaces), so reject any candidate that does not ('FLOOSIE' has 6 letters). Such clues often define one half of a famous name or phrase using the other half or a related word: 'floozy' + 'Flanders' -> 'Moll' (Moll Flanders), the 4-letter word that pairs with the clue word in the passage titles. Answer with only that missing word. If a bare number appears in parentheses, treat it only as this hint, not as part of the question.
- Double-meaning clues ('Term for an international match, or what its players are "put to"', 'X, or Y'): the answer is ONE word that satisfies BOTH halves ('the Test': a Test match; 'put to the test'). Check every candidate against both halves. A dictionary synonym that fits only one half ('trial') is wrong. When passages are noisy, use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
- A bare date + place (or date + event) fragment such as 'February 6, 1911 in Tampico, Illinois' asks for the person (or named thing) that the passages repeatedly tie to exactly that date and place, here the person born there that day. Give the bare name ('Ronald Reagan'), not the event, the place or the date.
- Jokes, asides and filler in the clue ('(If I eat it, can I hear the ocean?)', 'Need help in this subject? Call up...') are decoration. Answer from the factual core plus the anchor term. When the clue uses a local or foreign word ('In Haiti, lambi is this big spiral-shelled sea snail'), look for the passage that glosses it ('locally referred to as lambi') and answer with the common English name (Conch).

edits.target: Before the answer tags, briefly quote the matched line.
edits.content:
- ANSWER-FIRST layouts: list and flashcard pages often print the answer BEFORE the clue with no separator ('McCormick This spice company that owns Schilling is the largest producer of...', 'Garlic This relative of the onion is rarely grown from seed'). If the clue's text appears right after a short capitalized term, that term is the answer.
- Copy a verbatim answer exactly as shown, including its qualifier (state, numeral, title), and do not pad or trim it ('Anchorage, Alaska', not 'Anchorage'; 'McCormick', not 'McCormick & Company'). The verbatim form beats both the shortest-form advice in Rule 4 and any fuller official name found in other passages.

edits.target: Brief reasoning belongs before the tags.
edits.content: - Calibrate name length to a trivia answer key, using the short common form that the passages repeat. Drop corporate suffixes ('McCormick', not 'McCormick & Company'). Drop taglines or subtitles of shows and films when a short title is in common use ('Studio 60', not 'Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip'). Drop city, sponsor or year prefixes on a generic event when the clue says 'this <event>' ('the marathon', not 'Athens Classic Marathon'). Never cut a part that identifies the person: keep the regnal numeral of a king or of a play's title character ('Richard III', not 'Richard'; 'Henry V').

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- 'The energy / light / heat / force from this', 'this is measured by <instrument>' or 'caused by this' asks for the underlying SOURCE or object itself, as a plain noun ('the Sun'). Do not answer with a technical description of the energy or measurement ('direct solar radiation').
- Superlatives ('smallest in size', 'heaviest', 'oldest'): work out which dimension the clue asks about and compare ALL candidates on exactly that dimension. 'Smallest in size' means physical diameter, not denomination or value. The cent is worth the least, but the dime is physically the smallest U.S. coin in production. Do not answer with the item that is extreme in a different dimension.

edits.target: Choose the entity that recurs across many passages together with the clue's other named entities (e.g. the title in 'Thunder Road (film)' pages). Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - Epithet or attribution clues ('The New York Times Magazine has called him "King of the Techno-Thriller"', 'Critics dubbed her ...') ask for the PERSON. Find the passages that repeat the quoted epithet beside a name and answer with that full name as the passages write it ('Tom Clancy'). Ignore the publication or critic named in the clue.

edits.target: Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: A forum or quiz-thread line that reposts the clue and then offers the answer, even as a question to the host ('Alex, is that INVENTION?'), counts as an archive hit. Take that word.

edits.target: - A word in quotation marks inside the clue (a 'drag', a nickname) is usually a pun or hint tied to the answer. Look for passages where that word appears next to a candidate and answer with that candidate.
edits.content: - A word in quotation marks inside the clue (a 'drag', a nickname, 'steak') is usually a pun or hint tied to the answer. First identify the candidate from the plain factual descriptors ('Marquess', 'first 20th-century prime minister' -> Salisbury). Then use the pun as confirmation: passages where that word sits next to the candidate ('Salisbury steak') show it fits. Answer with the candidate, never the pun word.

edits.target: For people, prefer the form used in a verbatim answer from the context (Rule 3); otherwise use the name form most natural for the clue.
edits.content: - For kings, plays, characters and works, use the full standard name exactly as it recurs in the passage titles and headers, including regnal numerals, hyphens and a leading 'The' that belongs to the title ('Louis XIV', not 'Louis' or 'Louis Dieudonne'; 'Henry V'; 'Winnie-the-Pooh'; 'The Red Badge of Courage'). Quotation marks around the title do not matter.

edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content: - Match granularity. 'This film series / franchise / saga / show' wants the series name ('Scream'), not the particular installment the passages mostly discuss ('Scream 3') or its song. 'This subject in school' wants the general subject ('history'), not a sub-topic.
